Authentication Is Not Authorisation

On Thursday, investors paid a record $81.3bn for Anthropic's shares, and Wall Street still ended sharply lower. The same week, banks quietly settled a different question: who carries the risk when an AI agent acts?

Their answer: you do.

WHAT THE BANKS WROTE

JPMorgan and Bank of America moved in October. This month Citi added a new Section H to its online agreement, PNC changed its terms on 18 November, and Citizens emailed customers. Anything a third-party AI agent does now counts as the customer's act, including losses if the agent is hacked or leaks credentials. Citi exempts its own agents.

Fed Governor Barr said on 16 November that banks cannot verify whether an agent is genuine, whether the customer consented, or whether the action matches the instruction. Arizona has opened a preliminary criminal investigation into AI companies over apparent infiltration of banks by rogue agents.

THE GAP BEHIND THE CLAUSE

A bank can see a credential. It cannot see a mandate. So it assigns the loss to whoever holds the login, and the customer cannot grant limited, revocable authority because the plumbing for that does not exist. Customers hand over passwords. Banks hand back liability.

Authentication proves who is knocking. Authorisation defines what they may do.

YOU ARE THE CUSTOMER TOO

Inside a company, shared logins and borrowed human credentials put your institution in the customer's seat. Platform and vendor terms will increasingly say so. Even a founder's authority sits with the body that grants it: Nvidia's departed CEO said this week he would return only if the board decides, and the board said it does not intend to.

PAPER THE DELEGATION BEFORE SOMEONE ELSE PAPERS THE LIABILITY

◆ Give every agent its own identity. No shared passwords, no borrowed human logins.

◆ Scope the delegation: limits per action, per day and per counterparty, time-boxed and revocable.

◆ Read the liability clause in every platform and vendor agreement: who bears a loss when an agent acts with your credentials, and whose agents are exempt.

◆ Require named pre-approval for irreversible actions such as payments.

◆ Log what the agent was allowed to do and what it did, so a dispute is settled on evidence.

◆ Write the mandate down: an owner, limits, a stop condition and who answers.
A note on rigour: terms differ by bank, and whether consumer-protection rules cover agent transactions is contested. The Arizona probe is preliminary and Barr's remarks reach me through summaries. This is analysis, not legal advice.

No es una exageración. Es lo que ya dicen las condiciones de varios grandes bancos de EE. UU.

Esta semana Citi actualizó su acuerdo de usuario online: si das acceso a tu cuenta a un agente de IA de terceros, eres responsable de lo que haga. Y si ese agente filtra tus credenciales o lo hackean, también respondes tú de lo que hagan los atacantes.

👉 PNC ha cambiado sus condiciones en la misma línea.
👉 Citizens ha avisado por email a sus clientes de algo similar.

¿Qué me llevo, más allá de la banca?

1️⃣ La pregunta ya no es "¿qué puede hacer el agente?", sino "¿quién responde cuando se equivoca?".
2️⃣ Dar tus credenciales a una IA es como darle las llaves de casa a un desconocido muy listo. Cuando puedas, elige herramientas de solo lectura.
3️⃣ En la empresa pasa lo mismo: cada agente necesita permisos mínimos, un responsable humano y trazabilidad de lo que hace. Si no puedes reconstruir qué hizo y quién lo autorizó, el riesgo es tuyo.

Banks are reporting real gains from AI coding. Cutting engineering teams too quickly could limit what those gains are worth.

Bank of America reports a 20%+ improvement in general coding, with around 19,000 internal users. BNP Paribas puts developer productivity gains at 15%. Barclays reports a 15% improvement across the software development lifecycle.

At that scale, AI is freeing up meaningful capacity.

Having worked in product, I know how much valuable work sits in a bank’s backlog because engineering teams cannot get to it. An unreliable payment flow can remain unresolved while the team handles urgent maintenance.

AI gives banks room to tackle more of that work.

Yet some are already turning productivity gains into lower headcount. Barclays’ planned 5,000 job cuts include developer roles, with AI cited alongside wider technology improvements.

There is a trade-off here. Removing capacity as soon as it becomes available may leave a bank delivering roughly the same service at a lower cost.

I would give teams time to show what they can achieve with it first. Fixing problems that drive customers away could be worth more than the salaries saved.

In a landmark transaction, TCX and FMO - Dutch entrepreneurial development bank have joined forces to structure the first-ever offshore bond issuance denominated in Surinamese dollars (SRD), totaling approximately USD 100 million equivalent, across two maturities of 6 and 7 years.

Arranged by Bank of America (BofA) and listed on the Luxembourg Stock Exchange, this issuance represents an important milestone for the development of international capital markets in Surinamese dollars. Apart from the bonds, we were able to offset USD 24 mln in a 5 year swap format.

The transactions demonstrate the potential for frontier currencies to attract international investor interest, even at significant volumes and longer maturities. Importantly, it also enables TCX to recycle SRD currency risk into the capital markets, creating additional capacity to hedge future local-currency financing in #Suriname.

In October, we shared the first part of this story, when Suriname converted a USD 150 million IDB loan into Surinamese dollars, supported by an 18-year hedge. These notes are the second part, placing the first six and seven years of that exposure with international investors while we hold the longer-dated risk through 2044. 

This is how markets are built, by connecting international capital with local-currency financing needs, protecting borrowers’ debt service from currency risk, and opening the door to future transactions in frontier currencies.

A big thank you to our partners at FMO, Thierry De Malmazet De Saint Andéol Marc Otto and Bank of America Neha Gupta , and to the entire TCX team for making this landmark transaction possible!

Three big US banks just changed the rules on AI agents, and small business owners should pay attention.

This week Citi, PNC, and Citizens updated their customer terms: if a third-party AI agent connected to your account gets hacked, you eat the loss, not the bank. JPMorgan and Bank of America made the same move last month. Citi still takes responsibility when it's their own AI tools involved, just not yours.

If you run a small business, this is the liability question nobody was asking a year ago. You hand an AI assistant access to your banking, invoicing, or payments because it's convenient, and now the banks have made it clear where the risk sits if something goes wrong: with you.

I don't think that means ditching automation. It means building it with the right guardrails in place. Every automation I set up for clients treats money differently from everything else: agents can read, draft, and flag, but a person approves anything that actually touches funds. That one rule would cover you under these new terms no matter which bank you use.

If you've got AI tools connected to your business accounts, it's worth ten minutes to check what you're actually liable for.

Are you using AI agents anywhere near your business banking? What's made you comfortable with it, or held you back?

Big US banks now have a clear rule: if your AI agent loses your money, you pay.

According to recent reports, Citi changed its user agreement this week. If a customer gives an outside AI tool access to their bank account, the customer is responsible for everything the tool does. This includes mistakes. It also includes hacks. JPMorgan Chase, Bank of America and PNC have similar rules.

Our view: this is not only a bank story. It is a product design question for every team that adds AI agents to an app.

When an AI agent acts for a user, someone must answer one question: who pays if it fails? Now the answer is "the user". Users will see this. They will choose products where the agent can do less, but does it safely.

What we suggest to teams that build AI features:
— Start with read-only access. The agent can look, but not act.
— Ask the user to confirm every payment or important change.
— Give the agent its own limited access. Never the user's password.
— Save a clear record of every action the agent takes.

People will trust AI features because of clear limits, not big promises.
